entries.clue: Chair's feet I'd adjust for indoor natter (8,4)

indicatorNotes.adjust: To adjust a thing is to shift it out of the setting it arrived in, so these letters are not to be left standing where they were.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, the apostrophe counting for nothing
four more, the bits of furniture the surface is fiddling with
two letters, the contraction dropping its apostrophe as well

annotation.surface: Someone levelling up a wobbly chair by the feet.
annotation.walkthrough: Twelve letters of fodder sit in front of 'adjust', which leaves only the last two words to do any defining. A fireside chat takes its name from Franklin Roosevelt's radio broadcasts of the 1930s.
annotation.definitionFit: A fireside chat is a cosy informal talk by the hearth, and 'natter' is British for exactly that sort of relaxed chinwag.

indicatorNotes.Said: 'Said' asks for a word as it is spoken rather than as it is written, so what you hear comes out spelt another way.

blocks.note: to flee is to escape, and the two are said identically

annotation.surface: A report that somebody got away from a biting insect.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Said' points forward at 'to escape' rather than back at the insect, so the sound is taken from the verb and the noun is left to define. A flea can jump two hundred times its own body length.
annotation.definitionFit: A flea is a wingless blood-sucking insect that lives on mammals and birds, so 'insect' names it by its order.

entries.clue: Respond about two points and perform again (2-5)

indicatorNotes.about: What is placed about a thing has been wrapped round it, so the word named first closes over the letters named next.

blocks.note: to react is to respond to what has just happened
E is east and N is north, two of the four points on a compass card, taken in that order

annotation.surface: Someone answering on a couple of separate points before doing it all over again.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Points' reads as items on an agenda and means compass directions, which is nearly always its job in a cryptic. The hyphen in the enumeration falls exactly where the inserted pair begins.
annotation.definitionFit: To re-enact something is to perform it a second time — a battle re-enactment stages the fight again — so definition and answer are both verbs.

entries.clue: Chic and Steps on the radio (5)

indicatorNotes.on the radio: What comes over the radio is heard and never seen, so the word is wanted for its sound and not for its spelling.

blocks.note: a stile is the set of steps built over a wall or fence so that a British footpath can cross a field

annotation.surface: Two pop groups getting a mention on the radio.
annotation.walkthrough: Chic and Steps are both bands, which is what the capital letters are quietly buying; neither does any band work here. A stile is countryside furniture, two or three planks to climb a drystone wall by.
annotation.definitionFit: Chic and style are both nouns for elegance — she has style, she has chic — so the swap needs no change of form.

entries.clue: To unfasten part of bidet, a chore (6)

indicatorNotes.part of: A part of something is less than the whole of it, so only a run taken from inside the words that follow is wanted.

blocks.note: six letters running on unbroken from halfway into the first word, straight over the comma

annotation.surface: Taking a piece off the bidet, which is nobody's idea of a good afternoon.
annotation.walkthrough: Commas and word breaks are exactly where a buried run hides, and this one steps over both without a pause. 'To unfasten' is an infinitive, so the answer has to be one too.
annotation.definitionFit: To detach a thing is to unfasten it from whatever it was joined to — detach the coupon along the dotted line.

entries.clue: More cheeky spaniel I fenced in (7)

indicatorNotes.fenced in: To fence a thing in is to build a barrier all round it, so the letter beside the phrase is enclosed by the word before it.

blocks.note: a cocker is the spaniel bred to flush woodcock out of undergrowth
the pronoun taken as the single letter it is written with

annotation.surface: The speaker penning in a spaniel that was getting above itself.
annotation.walkthrough: 'More cheeky' demands a comparative, and the spaniel's name obligingly already ends in the -er that a comparative needs. Cocker spaniels are named for the woodcock, not for any swagger of their own.
annotation.definitionFit: Cocky means cheeky or over-confident, and the answer is its comparative, so it matches 'more cheeky' form for form.

entries.clue: An amount to cross annular island (5)

blocks.note: the indefinite article, in the form it takes before a consonant
the sum charged for crossing a bridge or a stretch of motorway

annotation.surface: The sum it costs to get across to a ring-shaped island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Amount to cross' looks like a single idea and is a charge levied for crossing, the sort collected at a toll bridge. 'Annular' simply means ring-shaped, from the Latin for a ring.
annotation.definitionFit: An atoll is the ring of coral left standing when the volcano it grew around sinks, so it is an island in the shape of a ring.

blocks.note: both little words introduce what a thing is about: news of the war, news concerning the war
a fence is the railing put round a field or a garden

annotation.surface: A crime committed against somebody's railing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Railing' can be a verb — ranting at something — and the surface leans that way; here it is the noun for what stands round a field. 'Concerning' is the commonest of the long words hiding a two-letter preposition.
annotation.definitionFit: An offence is any act the law punishes, from dropping litter upwards, so it and crime are interchangeable on a charge sheet.

indicatorNotes.vacant: A vacant room has had everything taken out of the middle of it, so the word keeps only the letters standing at its two ends.

blocks.note: Eve is the three-letter girl crosswords reach for first, the first woman of Genesis
the letters at the two ends of the word, with everything between them emptied out

annotation.surface: A row of girls, each of them staring into space.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Really vacant' reads as one phrase about the girl and splits into an adverb to be gutted and the instruction that guts it. Eve, Ada and Ena are the stock crossword girls when three letters are wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: Every and each both pick the members of a group out one at a time: every house on the street, each house on the street.

blocks.note: what a teacher does running down a register of names
a dressing-down, delivered to somebody who has stepped out of line

annotation.surface: A pupil counted as present and given a telling-off anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'But' pretends the two halves disagree when they are the same two words read twice over. The enumeration is the only warning that a phrase rather than a single word is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: To tick off a name is to put a tick beside it on a register, marking that person present; to tick somebody off is to reprimand them.

entries.clue: Bird to dance at Irish party, say (12)

indicatorNotes.say: 'Say' here asks for the sound of the words rather than their spelling, so what is heard gets written down another way.

blocks.note: to caper is to dance about, skipping and leaping
a ceilidh is a traditional Irish or Scottish evening of dancing to a fiddle, and the Gaelic spelling is said 'kay-lee'

annotation.surface: A bird throwing itself about at an Irish knees-up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' is doing sound work, not standing in for 'for example', which is the reading a solver tries first. The capercaillie is a turkey-sized grouse of the Scottish pine forests whose males gurgle and fan their tails at dawn.
annotation.definitionFit: The capercaillie is the largest of the grouse, a game bird of northern pine forest, so 'Bird' names it by its plainest category.

entries.clue: Day in the near future, rainy season (7)

blocks.note: Mon is how a diary shortens the first day of the working week
soon is what in the near future means

annotation.surface: A date coming up shortly, somewhere in the wet season.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Day' could be any of seven diary abbreviations, and only one of them leaves a word once the rest is stuck on the end. The monsoon is the seasonal reversal of wind that brings South Asia its summer rain.
annotation.definitionFit: Monsoon names the wet season itself as well as the wind behind it — 'the monsoon broke' means the rains arrived.

entries.clue: Partly concoct a new petrol ingredient (6)

indicatorNotes.Partly: Partly means not the whole of it, so a run of letters taken from inside the words that follow is all that is being offered.

blocks.note: six letters running on unbroken: the tail of the first word, all of the second, the start of the third

annotation.surface: A chemist halfway through mixing up a new fuel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Concoct' is the word begging to be an anagram indicator, and it is fodder instead — the letters lie in their given order and only need lifting out. The definition is the last two words and nothing else.
annotation.definitionFit: Octane is one of the hydrocarbons petrol is made of, so the definition names the answer by what it is a component of.

entries.clue: Relative maintains Irish victory for bliss (7)

indicatorNotes.maintains: To maintain a thing is to keep hold of it, and what a word keeps hold of is held inside it.

blocks.note: nana is the British child's word for a grandmother
IR is the two-letter short form of Irish
V is the letter Churchill's two raised fingers made, and the standard sign for victory

annotation.surface: A family member insisting an Irish win is the height of happiness.
annotation.walkthrough: In Buddhism nirvana is the blowing-out of desire and the end of rebirth, which is why 'bliss' is the loose everyday sense. 'Maintains' reads as 'claims' in the surface and means 'holds inside' in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Nirvana has slipped out of Buddhism into everyday English as a word for perfect bliss, the state nothing could improve on.

indicatorNotes.oddly: Oddly points at the odd-numbered letters, so the first, third, fifth and so on are taken and their neighbours left behind.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth and eleventh of the twelve letters, counted straight through the word breaks

annotation.surface: Somebody dancing strangely at a fashionable disco.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' sits where a solver expects it to describe the dancing; it is counting instead. The word breaks make no difference to that count — three words are treated as one unbroken string of twelve letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To frolic is to romp or caper about, which is dancing at its loosest; both are verbs for moving around out of sheer enjoyment.

indicatorNotes.twice: Twice asks for the instruction just given to be carried out a second time, so two different words for it are written one after the other.

blocks.note: to look is to observe
a second word for the same act, set down straight after the first

annotation.surface: An inspection in which everything gets checked a second time.
annotation.walkthrough: One word for observing will not fill seven letters, which is what 'twice' is there to solve. The hyphen in the enumeration marks the join between the two synonyms.
annotation.definitionFit: A once-over is a quick inspection — give the car the once-over — and a look-see is the same casual glance, both of them nouns.

indicatorNotes.away: Something taken away is gone, so the letter named just before it comes out of the word it was sitting in.

blocks.note: the metal loop hanging from a saddle that a rider's boot rests in
R is the standard one-letter short form of right, as in a stage direction

annotation.surface: Winding up a jockey's fan without any delay.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right away' reads as 'at once' and is two separate instructions, a letter and an order to remove it. A jockey's supporter is the iron the boot rests in, not a member of the crowd.
annotation.definitionFit: To stir up trouble is to provoke it, whipping into motion feeling that was lying quiet; both are transitive verbs.

entries.clue: Much fame for police officer breaking up smart do (12)

indicatorNotes.breaking up: Breaking a thing up leaves the pieces loose on the floor, so those letters are to be put back together in some other order.

blocks.note: the super is what a British police station calls its superintendent
seven letters re-set to follow the rank

annotation.surface: A police officer shutting down a rather posh party.
annotation.walkthrough: Breaking up a party is precisely what an officer does, which is why the phrase reads as action rather than as an order to shuffle letters. 'Super' is the rank below chief superintendent, familiar from every British police drama.
annotation.definitionFit: Superstardom is the condition of being a superstar, fame well past the ordinary sort, so 'Much fame' is naming the quantity rather than the kind.

blocks.note: p is how British prices write pence: 50p, and the coin itself is a p
E is the standard short form of English
the three-letter girl's name crosswords lean on hardest

annotation.surface: An English girl called Penny.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas make 'Penny, English girl' read as one person being introduced, when each of those three words is a separate piece. Penny is a girl's name and a coin, and the coin is the half that counts.
annotation.definitionFit: To peeve somebody is to irritate them; the participle 'peeved' is the commoner form, but both are verbs taking an object.

blocks.note: what a boxer does after a heavy punch, lurching without quite going down
the whirling Scottish and Irish ones, danced in sets of couples to a fiddle

annotation.surface: Somebody lurching his way from one dance to the next.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Through the' does no work beyond making a sentence out of two synonyms that are standing side by side. One spelling carries a drunkard's lurch and a Highland dance, and the clue asks you to hold both at once.
annotation.definitionFit: To reel is to stagger, as a drunk does; reels are also the brisk Scottish and Irish dances, so the same five letters answer both halves.

indicatorNotes.entertain: To entertain a guest is to have them inside the house, so the word does the same and takes the letter in.

blocks.note: an ass is a fool, the donkey standing in for the person
K is the king on a chessboard and in a pack of cards

annotation.surface: A jester called in to amuse the king.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Entertain' looks like the fool's job description and is the instruction to swallow a letter whole. Four letters is a tight space, so a three-letter fool and a one-letter king are close to forced.
annotation.definitionFit: To ask somebody round is to invite them — she asked us to dinner — so the two verbs match in sense and in form.

blocks.note: love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as the round letter
to pen something is to write it
an air is the old word for a tune or melody

annotation.surface: Someone who loves writing songs out in the garden.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Love' opens the clue looking like a verb and is the tennis nought. The definition is a single word at the end, and it has to cover a hyphenated compound, which the enumeration warns of before any letters arrive.
annotation.definitionFit: Open-air means out of doors: an open-air concert is one held outside, so the adjective and the definition do the same job.

indicatorNotes.away: What is taken away is gone for good, so the letter named just before it comes out of the word.

blocks.note: to erase is to remove a mark from a page
R is right's one-letter short form, the one used on maps and instructions

annotation.surface: A remedy that soothes and clears the trouble at once.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right away' reads as 'at once' and is really two instructions, a letter and an order to drop it. 'Removes' is the word being operated on, not the operation — that job belongs to 'away'.
annotation.definitionFit: To ease pain is to relieve it, lessening it rather than ending it, and both verbs take the same objects in the same form.

blocks.note: the straight half: an article of clothing, and one with a hyphen in its name
read as who the clothing is sold to, and meant as a description of the riders themselves, since the name says in two words what their legs spend the day doing

annotation.surface: Specialist clothing sold to people who ride bicycles.
annotation.walkthrough: Pedal-pushers are calf-length trousers, cut short so the hem stays clear of a bicycle chain, so the clue's joke is also the garment's etymology. The question mark admits the phrase is being read a second way.
annotation.definitionFit: Pedal-pushers are cropped trousers reaching mid-calf, and the name doubles as a plain description of cyclists, which is what the whole clue turns on.
